title: Cost of R&D tax credit study for a startup
description: This page explains what an R&D tax credit study costs a U.S. startup and how to judge that cost.
summary: This page explains what an R&D tax credit study costs a U.S. startup and how to judge that cost. Pricing ranges from contingency fees to hourly rates or software subscriptions, so startups should weigh total expected cost against the federal research credit retained, the payroll tax offset for qualified small businesses, and audit-ready documentation.

This report is general information, not tax or legal advice.
Key findings
For a startup, the cost of an R&D tax credit study only makes sense when weighed against the benefit the study supports and the audit exposure it leaves behind.
They are not IRS data, and HMRC's own figures do not show that claims prepared without a specialist agent fail more often.
Why R&D spending strains a startup budget

It identifies personnel (salaries, bonuses and stock-based compensation) as the largest cost, followed by software, prototyping materials, and facilities with specialized IT or laboratory capability, with rent, overhead and research-related travel as secondary items. It adds that financing R&D often involves convertible notes or warrants whose debt-or-equity classification is complex, and that investors read R&D outlays as indicators of growth potential and intangible-asset creation.
Federal incentives that a study supports
The Section 41 credit and the qualified research test

The research credit sits in IRC Section 41. Under Section 41(d)(1), as amended by Pub. L. 119-21 (July 4, 2025), qualified research must involve expenditures treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A, be undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature and intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component, and have substantially all of its activities form a process of experimentation for a functional purpose (function, performance, reliability or quality). Research related to style, taste, cosmetic or seasonal design factors does not qualify.

That is a common shorthand, but the statute expresses the first element as the Section 174A expenditure requirement and the business component requirement. The uncertainty element comes from the Section 174 regulations: Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) provides that uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product, or its appropriate design.
SBIR/STTR grants
SBIR.gov confirms that the SBIR and STTR programs use that name and are coordinated by the Small Business Administration, with eleven participating federal agencies funding the awards.
The payroll tax offset for qualified small businesses
Section 41(h) lets a qualified small business (QSB) elect to apply part of its research credit against employer payroll taxes.

items: QSB definition (Section 41(h)(3)): gross receipts below $5,000,000 for the taxable year, and no gross receipts in any taxable year before the 5-taxable-year period ending with that year. Tax-exempt organizations are excluded.

Cap: $250,000, increased by an additional $250,000 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022 (added by Pub. L. 117-169, the Inflation Reduction Act). The IRS confirms the election amount is $500,000 for those years. Practitioner sources (CLA, Adams Brown) describe the second $250,000 as usable against the employer share of Medicare tax.
Limits on use: the election cannot be made by a taxpayer that has made it for five or more preceding taxable years (Section 41(h)(4)).

Procedure: the election and amount are made on Form 6765 by the return due date, including extensions. The credit is then claimed on Form 8974 attached to Form 941 (or 943/944), starting with the first calendar quarter beginning after the income tax return is filed.

body.text: The statute's test is that the business had no gross receipts before the five-taxable-year period ending with the election year.
OBBBA and the Section 174A deduction

OBBBA (Pub. L. 119-21) was signed on July 4, 2025. It added Section 174A, which allows domestic research or experimental expenditures to be deducted currently (or, by election, capitalized and amortized) for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Eligible small businesses may elect to apply Section 174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, by amended returns or an automatic accounting method change, under procedures in Rev. Proc. 2025-28. Consultancy summaries (Aprio) describe eligibility as average annual gross receipts under $31 million for the three tax years preceding 2025.

items: Not a full repeal. Section 174 now covers foreign research or experimental expenditures, which must still be amortized over 15 years. Only domestic expenditures moved to immediate deduction.

The deduction and the credit are not fully additive. Amended Section 280C(c)(1) requires the Section 174A deduction to be reduced by the amount of the Section 41 credit, unless the taxpayer makes the irrevocable reduced-credit election under Section 280C(c)(2) on a timely return, in which case the credit itself is reduced instead.

Effective date conflict. One consultancy summary (Aprio) states that Section 174A applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2025. The statutory notes and EY state tax years beginning after December 31, 2024. The statute carries more weight, and this report follows it.

Audit exposure and its bearing on study cost
Where the failure-rate statistics come from

items: HMRC figures published alongside its 2022-23 annual report (July 2023) found 25% of sampled claims fully disallowed because no qualifying R&D took place and 19% containing an overclaim despite R&D being present. ICAEW reported that non-compliance by value was marginally higher where a specialist R&D agent was involved (25%) than where none was identified (24%).

HMRC's second programme (MREP2), in a report published October 30, 2024, found 30% of claims wholly non-compliant, 21% overclaimed and 49% compliant. Non-compliance by value was 28% for claims made with an agent and 21% for claims without one.

body.text: Documentation and Siemer Milling

The case is T.C. Memo. 2019-37, U.S. Tax Court Docket No. 21655-15, filed April 15, 2019 (Judge Buch). The court fully disallowed the research credits claimed for the tax years ended May 31, 2011 and 2012, finding the taxpayer had not shown its activities were qualified research, including a methodical plan of experimentation (drawing on Union Carbide). The credit studies had been prepared by an accounting firm from employee interviews and company documents. The court did not impose Section 6662 accuracy-related penalties, because the taxpayer had relied in good faith on that firm.
Failed projects
The regulations support the underlying principle: Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) states that the ultimate success, failure, sale or use of the product is not relevant to eligibility under Section 174.

items: 87% of R&D projects never reach production: Unverified.

SME error rate of 10.6%: this matches HMRC's estimate of error and fraud in the UK SME scheme for 2024-25 (£339 million), reported in its annual report of July 17, 2025 (per BDO). It is an error-and-fraud rate, not a measure of unclaimed relief. HMRC's 2025-26 annual report puts the 2023-24 SME scheme rate at 11.1%.

Analysis: what this means for a startup's study budget

This section is analysis, not a statement of law. The rules make the payroll offset the main route to cash for a pre-revenue startup, which means the study's value depends on the business meeting the QSB gross receipts test and on the credit surviving examination. Siemer Milling shows that a full disallowance can follow when a study rests on interviews and documents without evidence of a methodical experimentation process, so the documentation a study produces matters as much as its price. When comparing quotes, a startup should compare total expected cost (fee, internal time, and any defense coverage) against the credit retained, and should not rely on the UK failure-rate figures as a measure of US audit risk.
